BUSS1020 Week 11

BUSS1020 Week 11 — Simple Linear Regression and Model Fit

Regression, association and prediction

Regression models a numerical response Y using one or more predictors X. Simple regression has one predictor and one response; multiple regression has several predictors but still one response. A scatterplot places X horizontally and Y vertically to inspect positive or negative association, curvature and unusual observations. A lack of an obvious pattern does not rule out every possible relationship. Association alone does not establish causation.

A linear regression model is linear in its coefficients. Its predictors may include transformed variables; linearity in coefficients is not the same as requiring every predictor to appear without transformation.

Population model and sample fitted line

For observation i, the simple population model is:

Yᵢ = β₀ + β₁Xᵢ + εᵢ.

β₀ is the population intercept, β₁ the population slope, and εᵢ the unobserved random error. Xᵢ is the predictor and Yᵢ the response. For example, in a consumption model with disposable income as X, unmodelled influences such as prices are part of the error.

The conditional mean assumption E(ε|X) = 0 means that the error averages to zero at each predictor value. It implies the population regression line E(Y|X) = β₀ + β₁X. The notation E means expectation; the vertical bar means “conditional on”.

The equal-variance assumption Var(ε|X) = σ² says error variance is constant across X; it is called homoscedasticity. Independent errors and conditional normality support classical exact inference. Normality is not needed merely to calculate the fitted coefficients.

By iterated expectation, E(ε) = E[E(ε|X)] = 0. By the law of total variance, Var(ε) = E[Var(ε|X)] + Var[E(ε|X)] = σ² + 0 = σ². A constant's variance is zero.

From observed data (xᵢ,yᵢ), fit ŷᵢ = b₀ + b₁xᵢ. The sample estimates b₀ and b₁ estimate β₀ and β₁. The residual eᵢ = yᵢ − ŷᵢ is observable after fitting. The population error εᵢ = Yᵢ − E(Yᵢ|Xᵢ) is not directly observable because the true conditional mean is unknown.

Least squares

Ordinary least squares, abbreviated OLS, selects coefficients that minimise:

SSE = Σ(yᵢ − ŷᵢ)² = Σeᵢ².

Σ means sum over all n observations. Squaring vertical deviations prevents positive and negative residuals from cancelling and penalises larger deviations more strongly. “Best fitting” means smallest in-sample SSE among the candidate straight lines, not guaranteed best future predictions.

Define x̄ and ȳ as sample means, SSX = Σ(xᵢ − x̄)², and SSXY = Σ(xᵢ − x̄)(yᵢ − ȳ). For SSX > 0:

b₁ = SSXY/SSX = r(sᵧ/sₓ),

b₀ = ȳ − b₁x̄.

Here r is sample correlation and sₓ and sᵧ are sample standard deviations. Because sample covariance is SSXY/(n − 1), the slope also equals sample covariance divided by sample X variance. The fitted line passes through (x̄,ȳ).

For an intercept model, Σeᵢ = 0 is an algebraic result of OLS. It is not evidence that the population condition E(ε|X) = 0 is true.

The slope describes the change in predicted mean Y associated with a one-unit increase in X. The intercept is predicted Y at X = 0; it may have no meaningful interpretation if zero is impossible or far outside the observed range. Predictions at x₀ use ŷ₀ = b₀ + b₁x₀. The relevant range is the predictor range supported by observations; prediction outside it is extrapolation and may not preserve the relationship.

Decomposing variation

For an intercept OLS model:

Quantity

Formula

Meaning

Total sum of squares, SST

Σ(yᵢ − ȳ)² = (n − 1)sᵧ²

Variation around the sample mean

Regression sum of squares, SSR

Σ(ŷᵢ − ȳ)²

Variation explained by fitted values

Error sum of squares, SSE

Σ(yᵢ − ŷᵢ)²

Unexplained residual variation

SST = SSR + SSE. Here SSR means regression, not residual, sum of squares.

For nonconstant Y:

R² = SSR/SST = 1 − SSE/SST.

R² measures the fraction of observed response variation accounted for by the fitted model; 1 − R² = SSE/SST is the unexplained fraction. In intercept OLS, 0 ≤ R² ≤ 1. It is not the percentage of individual predictions that are correct and does not establish causation.

Multiple R = √R², which is nonnegative. In nondegenerate intercept regression it equals the correlation between observed and fitted responses. In simple regression it equals |r|, not necessarily signed r.

For nested intercept models using the same observations and response, adding predictors cannot increase the minimum SSE, so ordinary R² cannot fall. Adjusted R² penalises extra coefficients:

Adjusted R² = 1 − [SSE/(n − k − 1)]/[SST/(n − 1)].

k is the number of predictors excluding the intercept. Adjusted R² may rise or fall and may be negative; compare models fitted to the same response and observations rather than interpreting it as an ordinary raw percentage explained.

ANOVA and the residual error scale

Analysis of variance, abbreviated ANOVA, organises the variation and its degrees of freedom:

Degrees of freedom

Regression

MSR = SSR/k

MSE estimates the population error variance σ². The standard error of the estimate, also called SER or sₑ, is √MSE and estimates error standard deviation σ in response units. For simple regression, k = 1, residual df = n − 2, and sₑ = √[SSE/(n − 2)]. Sums of squares and degrees of freedom add across regression and residual rows; their mean squares do not.

Overall F test

F = MSR/MSE, with numerator df = k and denominator df = n − k − 1.

For simple regression, test H₀: β₁ = 0 against β₁ ≠ 0. For multiple regression, H₀ states that all k population slopes equal zero; H₁ states that at least one is nonzero. A significant overall result does not say that every predictor is individually significant.

Reject for a sufficiently large positive F: this is an upper-tail test even when the slope alternative is two-sided. The p-value is the upper-tail null probability. A 5% decision compares it with α = 0.05. This test assesses regression slopes, not equality of two population variances.

Worked examples

Example 1 — Sunflowers Apparel

For 14 stores, let Sales be annual sales in millions of dollars and Customers be profiled customers in millions. The fitted model is:

Predicted Sales = −1.209 + 2.074 × Customers.

A one-million increase in profiled customers is associated with $2.074 million higher predicted annual sales. The intercept predicts −$1.209 million at zero customers; its arithmetic meaning does not ensure business usefulness.

The correlation is approximately r = 0.921, R² = 0.8479, SER = 0.9993, and F = 66.879. About 84.79% of observed sales variation is accounted for by the linear model. The unexplained fraction is 1 − 0.8479 = 0.1521. SER corresponds to approximately $0.9993 million on the response scale. With k = 1 and n = 14, F uses df (1,12). Small discrepancies between squaring rounded r and the reported R² reflect rounding.

The sample means are x̄ = 1715 and ȳ = 286.5. SSX = 1,571,500, and SSXY = 172,500. Thus:

b₁ = 172,500/1,571,500 = 0.1097677,

b₀ = 286.5 − 0.1097677(1715) = 98.24833.

The fitted equation is ŷ = 98.24833 + 0.1097677x, often rounded to 98.24833 + 0.10977x. An extra square foot is associated with an increase of 0.1097677 thousand dollars, or about $109.77, in predicted mean price. A zero-area house is not meaningful, so the intercept should not be given a literal housing interpretation.

For x₀ = 2000 square feet:

ŷ₀ = 98.24833 + 0.1097677(2000) = 317.78381 thousand dollars, approximately $317,780 when rounded as 317.78 thousand dollars.

The observed predictor range is 1100 to 2450 square feet, so 2000 lies within it.

Using the residuals from the ten observations gives SSE = 13,665.5652. With residual df = 10 − 2 = 8:

MSE = 13,665.5652/8 = 1708.19565,

SER = √1708.19565 = 41.33032 thousand dollars.

The fitted statistics are R² = 0.58082, adjusted R² = 0.52842, F = 11.0848, and overall p = 0.01039. Regression, residual and total df are 1, 8 and 9. At 5%, reject a zero population slope: there is evidence of a linear association between floor area and price. The slope standard error is 0.03296944, a coefficient-uncertainty measure rather than the SD of area.

Example 4 — Regression to the mean

Regression to the mean describes the tendency for unusually extreme observations to be followed or accompanied by less extreme values when measurements are imperfectly correlated. In standardised simple regression, the predicted standardised response is r times the standardised predictor. When |r| < 1, its magnitude is smaller. This is a statistical tendency, not a guarantee for each individual, and does not by itself establish an effect of an intervention.

Excel implementation

Select Data → Data Analysis → Regression. Input Y Range is the response; Input X Range is one predictor column for simple regression or multiple predictor columns for multiple regression. Select Labels if headings are included and request residuals and standardised residuals for diagnosis. Preserve numerical precision and use scientific notation for very small p-values.

• DEVSQ(x_range) returns SSX.

• STEYX(y_range,x_range) returns simple-regression SER.

• TREND(y_range,x_range,new_x,TRUE) gives fitted predictions with an intercept. The response range comes first.

• Significance F is the overall F-test p-value.

• F.INV(1-alpha,k,n-k-1) returns the upper-tail critical value using the left-cumulative inverse.
